First step is to load libraries as always.

```{r}
#| label: Libraries setup
#| results: hide

#Load Libraries
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)
library(janitor)
```

Next we will load in the data and look it over.

```{r}
#| label: data import
#| results: hide

#pull in the data
intertidal_data <- read_csv(here("Week_09","Data","intertidaldata.csv"))

#make sure that quadrat and site is grouped as a factor
intertidal_data$Quadrat <- as.factor(intertidal_data$Quadrat)
intertidal_data$Site <- as.factor(intertidal_data$Site)

#count unique values in factor columns. Quadrat data is not clean. Will fix in next step.
unique(intertidal_data$Quadrat)
unique(intertidal_data$Site)

#load in the latitude data as well
intertidal_latitude_data <- read_csv(here("Week_09","Data","intertidaldata_latitude.csv"))

head(intertidal_data)
head(intertidal_latitude_data)
```

Before running an analysis, I need to clean the factors in the quadrat column.

```{r}
#| label: cleaning the data with janitor
#| results: hide

clean_intertidal_data <- intertidal_data|>
#factors are not clean. Low appears multiple times in different formats. Use make_clean_names function from janitor package.
mutate(Quadrat = make_clean_names(Quadrat,
                                  allow_dupes = TRUE),
       #manual change needed for the one typoed "mid" that Janitor can't clean
       Quadrat = recode(Quadrat,"mid_1" = "mid"),
       #use factor function to re-order manually
       Quadrat = factor(Quadrat,levels = c("low",
                                          "mid",
                                          "high")))|>
  #bring in latitude data
  left_join(intertidal_latitude_data,by = "Site")|>
  #reorder site factors by Latitude numeric value
  mutate(Site = fct_reorder(Site,Latitude))
  
  #make sure categories are clean and correctly ordered
  unique(clean_intertidal_data$Quadrat)
  unique(clean_intertidal_data$Site)

```

I want to do a simple boxplot visual showing the observed cover percentage of algae, broken down by the tide zone. I want to have boxplots for every site, and I want to use facet wrap to visualize the result.

```{r}
#| label: algae cover plot visual
#| results: hide
#| fig-cap: Figure 1
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 10

#create the plot
ggplot(clean_intertidal_data,aes(x = Quadrat,
                                 y = Algae,
                                 fill = Quadrat))+
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE)+
  #plot looks better with x-labels for all plots
  facet_wrap(~ Site,axes = "all_x")+
  #colorblind visual scheme
  scale_fill_viridis_d()+
  #make x-labels upper case
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Low",
                              "Mid",
                              "High"))+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 20,
                                  face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "aliceblue"))+
  labs(title = "Algae Cover by Quadrat Tide Classification",
       subtitle = "Sites Listed from South to North",
       x = "Tide Zone",
       y = "Relative Algae Cover (%)")

ggsave(here("Week_09","Outputs","Algae_Cover_Plot.jpg"))
```

The resultant data aligns with my expectations, which is a good sign that the data was correctly ordered for the plot. Quadrats in the low tide zone have significantly more algae cover in most of the sites. Only Cape Meares and Pyramid Point defy this trend. Most sites also show little to no algae cover in the high tide quadrats, which makes sense since these areas would be out of the water for large portions of the day.

Just for fun, let's create the exact same style plot visual, but analyzing rock cover.

```{r}
#| label: rock cover plot visual
#| results: hide
#| fig-cap: Figure 1
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 10

#create the plot
ggplot(clean_intertidal_data,aes(x = Quadrat,
                                 y = `Bare Rock`,
                                 fill = Quadrat))+
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE)+
  facet_wrap(~ Site,axes = "all_x")+
  scale_fill_viridis_d()+
  theme_minimal()+
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Low",
                     "Mid",
                     "High"))+
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 20,
                                  face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "aliceblue"))+
  labs(title = "Rock Cover by Quadrat Tide Classification",
       subtitle = "Sites Listed from South to North",
       x = "Tide Zone",
       y = "Relative Rock Cover (%)")

ggsave(here("Week_09","Outputs","Rock_Cover_Plot.jpg"))
```

In this case, the bare rock cover present in the low tide zones is very low, almost zero. My assumption is that the constant presence of water here means that a wide variety of intertidal organisms thrive here. However, bare rock does not necessarily rise in cover percentage in high tide plots. Something else must be living in this zone. Perhaps barnacles?

```{r}
#| label: barnacle cover plot visual
#| results: hide
#| fig-cap: Figure 1
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 10

#I want to lump small and large barnacles together in a single column
clean_intertidal_data <- clean_intertidal_data|>
  mutate(Barnacles = `Large Barnacles`+ `Small Barnacles`)

#create the plot
ggplot(clean_intertidal_data,aes(x = Quadrat,
                                 y = Barnacles,
                                 fill = Quadrat))+
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE)+
  facet_wrap(~ Site,axes = "all_x")+
  scale_fill_viridis_d()+
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Low",
                              "Mid",
                              "High"))+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 20,
                                  face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 10,
                                    face = "italic"),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "aliceblue"))+
  labs(title = "Barnacle Cover by Quadrat Tide Classification",
       subtitle = "Sites Listed from South to North",
       x = "Tide Zone",
       y = "Relative Barnacle Cover (%)",
       caption = "Small and large barnacles added together for analysis")

ggsave(here("Week_09","Outputs","Barnacle_Cover_Plot.jpg"))
```

Barnacle cover is generally highest in the high tide zone. At Shell Beach, Starfish Point, Crystal Cove, and Dana Point, it is by far the dominant cover type in the high tide zones. I assume these are rocky substrates where the barnacles can establish. However, sites like Bodega, Cambria, Hazards, and Little Corona, barnacle cover remains at or near zero even as tide zone changes. I assume the substrate here is not conducive to barnacles. It appears that site-specific environmental factors interact with tide zone to determine species cover, and both are important.
